cls: Thienopyridine antiplatelet agent (P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonist)
pharm: Irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, inhibiting ADP-induced platelet aggregation and fibrinogen binding to the GP IIb/IIIa complex for the life of the platelet
quick: 250 mg orally twice daily with food
Take with food to improve absorption and reduce GI upset
Avoid unless clearly needed; safety not established
Avoid; excreted in animal milk, human data lacking
Use with caution; consider dose reduction in significant impairment
Avoid in severe hepatic impairment; hepatically metabolized
CBC with differential every 2 weeks for first 3 months; signs of bleeding, TTP
summary: Ticlopidine hydrochloride is an oral thienopyridine antiplatelet drug that irreversibly inhibits the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. It has been used to reduce the risk of thrombotic stroke in patients intolerant of aspirin and, with aspirin, to prevent stent thrombosis. Its use is now largely historical and it has been discontinued/superseded in the US by clopidogrel and prasugrel because of a boxed warning for life-threatening hematologic toxicity - neutropenia/agranulocytosis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and aplastic anemia - requiring frequent blood-count monitoring.
indications: Reduction of the risk of thrombotic stroke in patients who have had a stroke or stroke precursors and are intolerant of or have failed aspirin therapy
With aspirin, prevention of subacute stent thrombosis after coronary stent implantation (historical use)

dosage.d: 250 mg orally twice daily with food
dosage.n: Take with meals to improve tolerance and bioavailability

dosage.d: 250 mg orally twice daily with food plus aspirin, for up to 30 days after stenting (historical regimen)

admin: Take orally twice daily with food to maximize absorption and minimize gastrointestinal upset
Obtain a baseline CBC with differential, then monitor every 2 weeks from the start of therapy through the end of the third month
Discontinue immediately if neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, or features of TTP develop
Stop about 10-14 days before elective surgery (irreversible platelet effect)
Counsel patients to report fever, sore throat, mucosal bleeding/bruising, pallor, jaundice, or neurologic symptoms
moa: Ticlopidine is a thienopyridine prodrug whose active metabolite irreversibly inhibits the platelet P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor. This blocks ADP-induced activation of the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa complex and fibrinogen binding, inhibiting platelet aggregation for the lifespan of the affected platelet (about 7-10 days). The effect is not immediate; maximal platelet inhibition develops over several days.

absolute: Hematopoietic disorders such as neutropenia or thrombocytopenia
Presence of a hemostatic disorder or active pathological bleeding (e.g. bleeding peptic ulcer, intracranial bleeding)
Prior history of TTP or aplastic anemia attributed to ticlopidine
relative: Increased risk of bleeding (trauma, surgery, ulcer history)
Concomitant anticoagulants or other antiplatelet agents
monitor: CBC with differential every 2 weeks for the first 3 months
Signs of bleeding and of TTP (fever, neurologic changes, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, renal dysfunction)

preg: There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Ticlopidine should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit clearly justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Ticlopidine is excreted in the milk of lactating animals; it is not known whether it is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in the infant, a decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, taking into account its importance to the mother.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; plasma clearance is reduced and dosage reduction may be necessary in significant impairment. There is limited experience in severe renal disease.
hepatic: Ticlopidine is extensively metabolized by the liver. It is contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment and should be used with caution in lesser hepatic dysfunction; cholestatic hepatitis has been reported.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs) - markedly increased bleeding risk; avoid or monitor closely
Other antiplatelet agents / NSAIDs - additive bleeding risk
Theophylline - ticlopidine reduces theophylline clearance, raising levels (risk of toxicity)
moderate: Phenytoin - ticlopidine can increase phenytoin levels (CYP inhibition)
Cyclosporine - ticlopidine may decrease cyclosporine blood levels
minor: Digoxin - slight decrease in digoxin plasma levels
interactions.food: Take with food (improves absorption and tolerability); antacids reduce absorption
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol (additive gastrointestinal irritation and bleeding risk)
interactions.diagnostics: Prolongs bleeding time; may cause elevated alkaline phosphatase/transaminases and elevated serum cholesterol/triglycerides

monitoring: CBC with white-cell differential and platelet count every 2 weeks from start through the third month of therapy (and promptly if symptoms suggest cytopenia)
Signs/symptoms of TTP - fever, neurologic changes, thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, renal dysfunction
Liver function tests if hepatic dysfunction suspected
counsel: Take twice daily with food and have your blood counts checked every 2 weeks for the first 3 months - do not skip these tests
Urgently report fever, chills, sore throat, mouth ulcers, unusual bruising or bleeding, pale or yellow skin, dark urine, or confusion/weakness
Tell any doctor or dentist that you take this blood-thinning medicine before any surgery or procedure
Avoid other blood thinners, aspirin, or anti-inflammatory painkillers unless your clinician approves
Do not stop the medicine suddenly without medical advice
pk: Delayed - antiplatelet effect develops over days; maximal inhibition typically by 8-11 days
Peak plasma concentration about 2 hours after an oral dose (absorption increased with food)
Terminal elimination half-life about 12 hours after a single dose, lengthening to ~4-5 days with repeated dosing
Irreversible platelet inhibition lasting the platelet lifespan; bleeding time normalizes about 1-2 weeks after stopping
Store at controlled room temperature, 20-25 C (68-77 F), in a tight container
pearls: BOXED WARNING: ticlopidine causes life-threatening hematologic reactions - neutropenia/agranulocytosis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and aplastic anemia - mandating CBC with differential every 2 weeks for the first 3 months

Not currently FDA-marketed (US-discontinued) and largely superseded by clopidogrel and prasugrel, which have a far better safety profile. This record is based on the historical US prescribing information, BNF, and SmPC data.
Reserve for patients intolerant of or who fail aspirin; the antiplatelet effect is delayed (days) and irreversible for the platelet lifespan
Stop about 10-14 days before elective surgery because of irreversible platelet inhibition
Stop immediately and investigate for fever, sore throat, mucosal bleeding, pallor, jaundice, or neurologic symptoms - features of agranulocytosis or TTP
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose - do not take a double dose. Maintaining consistent twice-daily dosing is important for sustained antiplatelet effect.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Reported effects (from animal data and case reports) include increased bleeding time, gastrointestinal upset, and possibly hemorrhage. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: protect the airway, manage bleeding with local measures and platelet transfusion if needed (since the platelet effect is irreversible), and provide general supportive care; methylprednisolone has been used to shorten bleeding time in some reports.
